title: Korea, Japan, Singapore race to lead floating data centers amid AI power crunch
source_used: Chosunbiz (full text from the main session's fulltext copy)
key_facts: Shipbuilders in Korea, Japan and Singapore form the lead group in floating data centres (FDC), which need no large tracts of land and can use seawater for cooling.
Chosunbiz says economic viability needs further verification: there is no standard design, design and construction costs are high, and servers must run stably amid salinity, humidity and waves.

Singapore: Keppel, reviewing the business since 2019 and approved by the government in 2023, signed long-term contracts with global big tech firms and began building a 25 MW floating data centre this year, to start in 2028; Seatrium won an approval in principle from Bureau Veritas in July for a 30 MW unit.
Japan: shipping company MOL began a project in March with Hitachi and Hitachi Systems to convert secondhand ships into floating data centres, targeting operations in 2027.

Korea: Samsung Heavy Industries is developing a 50 MW unit with the US developer M3 (engineering contract signed in August, main EPC contract being pursued); HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering began work with Schneider Electric in July; Hanwha Ocean unveiled a 60 MW design at Gastech 2026 in Bangkok and received American Bureau of Shipping certification.
Europe is dispersing data centres to Northern and Southern Europe where power is easier to secure; China has a subsea data centre off Shanghai, powered by offshore wind, operating this year.
Industry watchers expect it to take considerable time before this becomes a revenue source for shipbuilders; a shipbuilding official says the key is matching onshore stability and utilization rates.
quote_evidence: But economic viability appears to need further verification.
Industry watchers expect it will take considerable time before this becomes a new revenue source for the shipbuilding and offshore sectors.
Even in the United States, building land-based data centers faces difficulties due to permits and local opposition, so floating data centers are seen as a promising business.
why_it_matters_hint: Land and power are limiting new AI data centres, so shipbuilders are testing sea-based sites, but costs and stability are unproven and the first units are due in 2027 and 2028.
event_date: 12 Oct 2026 (Chosunbiz, 'according to the industry on the 12th')
notes: Single outlet, most claims are company or official statements quoted by Chosunbiz and not independently checked. The last quote_evidence line is a Samsung Heavy Industries official quoted by Chosunbiz.
